rm-one-file.title: Delete One Exact File Safely
rm-one-file.bodyMarkdown:
`rm` removes a file at the path you give it. Terminal deletion deserves extra care because `rm` commonly removes the file directly instead of placing it in a desktop Trash or Recycle Bin.

A safe routine is to inspect first:

```text
$ ls
notes.txt  temp.log
```

If `temp.log` is the exact disposable file, remove only that name:

```bash
rm temp.log
```

Then run `ls` again and confirm that `notes.txt` remains while `temp.log` is gone.

The important skill is not typing `rm` quickly; it is being certain about the target before pressing **Enter**. In this course, avoid recursive removal flags and broad wildcards so one command cannot accidentally reach many files.

move-to-trash-alternative.title: When Unsure, Move to Review
move-to-trash-alternative.bodyMarkdown:
If you are unsure whether a file can be deleted, do not use `rm` yet. A safer choice is to move the file into a holding folder so it stays available while you review it.

For example:

```text
$ mkdir -p review
$ mv old-notes.txt review/old-notes.txt
$ ls review
old-notes.txt
```

First, `mkdir -p` makes sure the holding folder exists. Then `mv` preserves the uncertain file by relocating it, and `ls review` verifies its new location.

This is not the same as the operating system's Trash. It is a deliberate filesystem workflow that keeps the file available. When you are uncertain, preserve first and confirm where the file went before considering permanent deletion.
